Allah mentioned the disbelievers, then divided them into two categories: the People of the Book and the polytheists. He mentioned that all of them would not be separated (from their state) until the clear proof came to them, and the establishment of the argument against them through the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

As for the meaning of "munfakkin" (separated): it means "separated" (munfasilin). Then scholars differed about the sense of this separation, into four opinions:

The first: the meaning is that they would not be separated from their disbelief until there came to them (a messenger) so that the argument would be established against them.

The second: they would not be separated from knowledge of the prophethood of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) until Allah sent him.

The third, chosen by Ibn 'Atiyya: they would not be separated from the observation of Allah and His power, until Allah sends to them a messenger who establishes the argument against them.

The fourth, which is the most apparent to me: the meaning is that they would not cease from the world until Allah sent to them our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and the argument was thereby established against them. For had they died without his being sent, they would have said: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134]. So when Allah sent him, no excuse or argument remained for them. Thus "munfakkin" in this sense is like your saying: "He will not leave (or cease) until such-and-such occurs."

﴿A messenger from Allah﴾, meaning our master Muhammad (ﷺ). Its grammatical analysis (i'rab): it is either a substitute (badal) for "the clear proof," or the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar mubtada' mudmar), meaning "he is a messenger from Allah."

﴿Reciting purified pages﴾, meaning the Qur'an in its pages.

﴿Within them are upright books﴾, i.e., upright in truth, correct in meanings. The morphological pattern (wazn) of "qayyima" is "fay'ala," and it carries the sense of emphasis (mubalagha). Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is by omission of a modifier, its meaning being: "within them are the rulings of books." But this does not need such omission, because "al-kutub" here means "the written things" (al-maktubat).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 98, verses 4–7:

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after clear evidence had come to them.﴾ That is, they did not differ about the prophethood of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) except after they had come to know that it is true. It may also be that He means their division in their religion, as in His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Scripture, but it was disputed over.﴾ [Fussilat: 45]. The reason the People of the Scripture are singled out here, after being mentioned together with others at the beginning of the surah, is that they knew the truth of the prophethood of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) from what they found in their books concerning him. ﴿And they were not commanded﴾: the meaning here is: they were commanded in the Torah and the Gospel only to worship Allah, but they distorted or altered (it). It may also be that the meaning is: they were commanded in the Qur'an only to worship Allah, so for what reason do they deny it and disbelieve in it? ﴿sincere in devotion to Him, upright﴾. The Malikis used this to establish that intention is obligatory in wudu'. This is far-fetched, because sincerity (ikhlas) here means monotheism and abandoning association (shirk), or abandoning showing off (riya'). Sincerity is required both in monotheism and in actions. Sincerity in monotheism is the clear shirk, and sincerity in actions is the hidden shirk, which is showing off (riya'). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Showing off is the minor shirk." And he (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord, that He, Exalted is He, says: "I am the most self-sufficient of partners, so whoever does an action in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his partner."

Know that actions are of three kinds: commanded, forbidden, and permissible. As for commanded acts, sincerity in them means purity of intention for the sake of Allah's countenance, such that it is not mixed with any other intention. If it is so, the act is sincere and accepted. If the intention is other than the countenance of Allah, such as seeking a worldly benefit, or praise, or something else, then the act is pure showing off and rejected. If the intention is mixed, there is detail in this which requires consideration and is open to possibility. As for forbidden acts, if one abandons them without intention, he is discharged of the obligation but gains no reward for abandoning them; and if he abandons them with the intention of Allah's countenance, he is discharged of the obligation together with reward. As for permissible acts, such as eating, sleeping, intercourse and the like, if one does them without intention, there is no reward in them; and if one does them with the intention of Allah's countenance, he has reward in them. Every permissible act can become an act of devotion when it is intended for Allah's countenance, such as intending by eating the strength to worship, and intending by intercourse to guard oneself from what is unlawful.

﴿ḥunafā'﴾ is the plural of ḥanīf, and it has been mentioned. ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾: its estimate is "the upright community" or "the upright congregation." We have explained the meaning of "upright" (qayyima): that what they were commanded, namely worshipping Allah, sincerity toward Him, establishing prayer and giving zakat, is the religion of Islam. So for what reason do they not enter into it? ﴿the best of creation (al-bariyyah)﴾: creation, because Allah originated them and brought them into existence after non-existence. It was read with the hamza, which is the original form, and with the yā' (al-biyyah), which is a lightening of the hamzated form, and it is more commonly used among the Arabs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 98, verse 8:

﴿Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him﴾. It is disputed whether this refers to the present world or to the Hereafter. Their being pleased with Allah in this world is their contentment with His decree (al-qada') and their contentment with His religion (din). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has tasted the flavor of faith is one who is pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad as Messenger." Their being pleased with Him in the Hereafter is their contentment with what Allah has given them therein, or Allah's being pleased with them, as is related in the hadith that Allah says: "O people of Paradise, do you want anything more that I may give you?" They will say: "O our Lord, what more could we want, when You have given us what You have given no one else among the worlds?" He will say: "I have something better than that: My pleasure. I will never be displeased with you again."

﴿That is for one who fears his Lord﴾. That is, for one who fears Him. This is evidence of the virtue of fear. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The fear of Allah is the head of all wisdom."
